Storm surge is the rise in seawater level caused solely by a storm, measured as the height of the water above the normal predicted astronomical tide. [NOAA-SURGE](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/stormsurge-stormtide.html)
Storm tide is the total observed seawater level during a storm, resulting from the combination of storm surge and the astronomical tide. [NOAA-SURGE](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/stormsurge-stormtide.html)
The surge is caused primarily by a storm's winds pushing water onshore. [NOAA-SURGE](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/stormsurge-stormtide.html)
The amplitude of the storm surge at any given location depends on the orientation of the coast line with the storm track, the intensity, size, and speed of the storm, and the local bathymetry. [NOAA-SURGE](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/stormsurge-stormtide.html)
The highest storm tides are often observed during storms that coincide with a new or full moon. [NOAA-SURGE](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/stormsurge-stormtide.html)
This frozen page is not a current storm forecast.

aspect_rubric.cause and local factor: Primary cause is storm winds pushing water onshore. Accept at least one location-dependent factor named by NOAA, such as coastline orientation relative to the track or local bathymetry; do not treat this frozen page as a current forecast.
aspect_rubric.definitions: Storm surge is abnormal storm-caused seawater rise above the predicted astronomical tide. Storm tide is the total observed level during a storm: surge plus the normal astronomical tide.

claims.text: Storm surge is the rise in seawater level caused solely by a storm, measured as the height of the water above the normal predicted astronomical tide.
Storm tide is the total observed seawater level during a storm, resulting from the combination of storm surge and the astronomical tide.
The surge is caused primarily by a storm's winds pushing water onshore.
The amplitude of the storm surge at any given location depends on the orientation of the coast line with the storm track, the intensity, size, and speed of the storm, and the local bathymetry.
The highest storm tides are often observed during storms that coincide with a new or full moon.

limitations: This frozen page is not a current storm forecast.
cases.question: According to the frozen NOAA page, distinguish storm surge from storm tide, identify the main cause of surge, and name one local factor affecting its height.

Observers on Earth see the same face of the Moon all the time because the Moon rotates just once on its own axis in very nearly the same time that it travels once around Earth, a phenomenon called synchronous rotation. [NASA-MOON, p.2](https://science.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/62217main-moon-lithograph.pdf#page=2)
The light areas on the near side are lunar highlands. [NASA-MOON, p.2](https://science.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/62217main-moon-lithograph.pdf#page=2)
The dark features, called maria, are impact basins that were filled with dark lava between 4 and 2.5 billion years ago. [NASA-MOON, p.2](https://science.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/62217main-moon-lithograph.pdf#page=2)
The 2001 lithograph is historical; its mission counts are not current facts.

aspect_rubric.same lunar face: The lithograph attributes the nearly fixed Earth-facing side to synchronous rotation: the Moon rotates about once in the time it travels around Earth.
aspect_rubric.surface regions: Bright areas are lunar highlands. Dark maria are impact basins filled with dark lava; the handout dates this filling to roughly 4 to 2.5 billion years ago. Do not promote its 2001 mission counts into a current claim.

The dark features, called maria, are impact basins that were filled with dark lava between 4 and 2.5 billion years ago.

cases.question: According to NASA's dated Moon lithograph, why do observers on Earth see nearly the same lunar face, and how does the text distinguish bright highlands from dark maria?
